messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The fire started in the janitor’s storage closet on a Tuesday afternoon. Eleanor was still in her office, reviewing a student’s schedule, when the smoke alarms began to scream. She had been a school counselor for forty-three years, first at a middle school in Ohio and then, after her husband passed, at a high school just outside Portland. She knew every hallway, every exit, every fire drill protocol by heart. But on that day, what she had not anticipated was the crush of bodies in the main corridor—students pushing, shouting, someone falling near the east stairwell. Eleanor had tried to direct them toward the south exit, but a young man, frantic, had shoved her hard into the lockers. She hit her head, went down, and for a long, terrible moment the crowd moved over her. She remembered the weight of shoes, the smell of smoke and sweat, the certainty that she would die there, trampled by children she had spent her life trying to protect.

In the months that followed, Eleanor found she could not stop thinking about the unfairness of it. What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, she thought, again and again. The school had held a brief assembly, called it a "drill gone wrong," and moved on. No one had apologized. No one had been held accountable. She had come to believe that the world had shown its true face—indifferent, chaotic, and cruel—and that the person she had been, the happy, steady counselor who believed in second chances, had been erased. I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable, she told herself. She felt like she didn't know herself anymore, as though the woman who had once laughed with teachers and calmed crying teenagers had been replaced by someone brittle and watchful.

That watchfulness became a constant companion. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home—the creak of a floorboard, the click of the furnace—and found herself unable to relax even when she knew she was in a safe place. The world felt dangerous now because it had proven itself to be unfair, and if it was unfair, then anything could happen at any time. She jumped or startled at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people: a car door slamming, a dropped book in the library, the sudden ring of a telephone. Each startle confirmed what she already believed—that she was no longer safe, that she had lost the right to feel at ease.

To cope, Eleanor began to drink. A glass of wine after work became two, became three. She also took her late husband’s old sleeping pills on nights when her mind would not stop circling. She found herself ruminating about how to get even with the assailant—the young man who had shoved her—though she did not know his name. She imagined writing a letter, filing a report, standing in front of the school board and demanding justice. But she never did. Instead, she stayed near exits everywhere she went—the grocery store, the church, the doctor’s waiting room—always scanning for the quickest way out. These strategies, she believed, were the only things keeping her from falling apart entirely. But they also deepened her isolation. She stopped meeting friends for coffee because the café had only one door. She retired early from counseling because the school itself had become a trigger. And as she withdrew, her belief that she had lost herself grew stronger. She was certain she would never be the same, and that certainty made her more vigilant, more afraid.

At night, alone in the house she had once shared with her husband, Eleanor would sit in the living room with the lights off, listening. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, and when she heard nothing, she listened harder. The silence itself felt threatening. She could not relax. She could not sleep. She could not stop thinking about the injustice. The more she drank, the more she ruminated. The more she ruminated, the more she believed she was broken. And the more she believed she was broken, the more she listened for danger. It was a circle that tightened every day.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the grocery store. A child ran past her, laughing, and Eleanor dropped to her knees, covering her head. She stayed there on the linoleum floor for nearly a minute while strangers stared. That night, she called a clinic. She did not know if therapy could undo what had happened. She was certain it probably could not. But she was afraid of what she might become if she did not try.
